title: Speech Therapy Billing Codes: 2027 Treatment Code Changes and SLP and OT Evaluation CPT Codes
summary: Speech therapy billing codes change January 1, 2027, when 92507 is replaced by 10 timed treatment codes. Plus the SLP and OT evaluation CPT codes and what notes must show.
body_markdown:
Accurate CPT codes are essential for documenting evaluations and treatments. For speech-language pathology, starting January 1, 2027, CPT code 92507 will be replaced by 10 time-based codes organized into five clinical categories.


According to[ASHA](https://www.asha.org/practice/reimbursement/coding/new-speech-language-pathology-treatment-codes-replacing-92507/treatment-codes/) , the five categories and their new codes are:


Category What it covers Base code (first 30 minutes) Add-on code (each additional 15 minutes)


Fluency Stuttering, cluttering, and other breaks in the flow of speech **92654** **92655**


Speech sound production Producing speech sounds clearly, including motor speech problems **92656** **92657**


Language comprehension and expression Understanding and using language **92658** **92659**


Speech sound production and language combined Speech sounds and language treated in the same session **92660** **92661**


Voice, upper airway dysfunction, and resonance Problems with the voice, the upper airway, or resonance **92662** **92663**


All 10 codes are for one-on-one treatment. An add-on code is always billed with its matching base code, never on its own. Group treatment (two or more people) stays on 92508, which remains untimed.


Why? According to[ASHA](https://www.asha.org/practice/reimbursement/coding/new-speech-language-pathology-treatment-codes-replacing-92507/background/) , a CMS review of Medicare utilization for CPT code 92507 found that use of the code increased by more than 100% between 2017 and 2022. That increase prompted additional payer scrutiny and a reassessment of the code's structure and valuation.


Whether the setting is a school, home, or skilled nursing facility, SLPs and OTs rely on clinical reasoning to capture a patient's baseline, document the precise level of help required, and track improvement.


Clinicians are busy evaluating how the new time increments may affect daily scheduling, productivity tracking, and insurance authorization limits, as well as how private payers may authorize multiple codes during one session—or how National Correct Coding Initiative (NCCI) edits may affect billing for overlapping treatment categories.


## Which CPT Code Does a Speech Therapy Evaluation Use, and What Must the Note Show?


The speech therapy evaluation CPT code is one of four untimed codes, billed as one unit no matter how long the evaluation takes: 92521 for fluency, 92522 for speech sound production, 92523 for speech sound production plus language, and 92524 for voice and resonance. The note must show the clinical findings for that area, a diagnosis, and treatment recommendations.


These codes aren't changing in 2027. A few SLP evaluations are timed: the aphasia assessment (96105) is billed per hour, and AAC device evaluations (92605 and 92607) are billed by the first hour, with add-on codes for each additional 30 minutes. For the treatment code change, see[ASHA's guide to the new codes replacing 92507](https://www.asha.org/practice/reimbursement/coding/new-speech-language-pathology-treatment-codes-replacing-92507/treatment-codes/) .


Evaluation Code Description What the Report Must Show


**92521** Evaluation of speech fluency Type and frequency of disfluencies, secondary behaviors, impact on communication, diagnosis, and treatment recommendations


**92522** Evaluation of speech sound production (articulation, phonological process, apraxia, dysarthria) Sound errors and error patterns, intelligibility, stimulability, diagnosis, and treatment recommendations


**92523** Evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression Speech sound findings plus receptive and expressive language findings, diagnosis, and treatment recommendations


**92524** Behavioral and qualitative analysis of voice and resonance Perceptual voice and resonance findings, vocal behaviors, relevant medical history or instrumental results, diagnosis, and treatment recommendations


Speech therapy billing codes tell the payer what service was provided, but payers decide on funding for specialized services and equipment based largely on two documents: the evaluation report and the physician's order. The evaluation report has to show the clinical findings that justify the service or device. The physician's order has to state that the service or device is medically necessary and list the diagnosis codes it is based on. Those diagnosis codes should match the diagnosis in the evaluation report. If either document is missing that information, or the two don't agree, authorization can be delayed or denied.


This matters most for augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices. The evaluation should connect the patient's communication deficits to the specific device being recommended and explain why it is medically necessary. The physician's order should then state that necessity and list the same diagnosis codes.


## Occupational Therapy Evaluation CPT Codes by Complexity Level


The occupational therapy evaluation CPT code is 97165 (low), 97166 (moderate), or 97167 (high complexity). These codes aren't changing in 2027. The level depends on three components: the occupational profile and history, the performance deficits found, and clinical decision-making.


Per[AOTA guidelines](https://www.aota.org/) , the lowest-scoring component sets the level. If two components qualify as high complexity but one falls into low complexity, the entire evaluation is billed at the low-complexity level.


CPT Code/Level Profile and History Performance Deficits Clinical Decision Making


Low complexity (97165) Brief history of the current problem; related records reviewed **1 to 3** deficits, each linked to an everyday activity Focused assessment; a few treatment options; no conditions affecting function; no help needed to finish the evaluation


Moderate complexity (97166) Broader records review; added physical, cognitive, or psychosocial history **3 to 5** deficits, each linked to an everyday activity Detailed assessment; several treatment options; other conditions may affect function; some task changes or help needed


High complexity (97167) Full records review; in-depth physical, cognitive, or psychosocial history **5 or more** deficits, each linked to an everyday activity Comprehensive assessment; many treatment options; other conditions affect function; significant task changes or help needed


## Timed and Untimed Codes, Minutes, and Documentation


CMS splits therapy codes into two types:


- Untimed codes: Billed once per session regardless of duration.
- Timed codes: Vary based on direct, one-on-one treatment minutes.


The CMS 8-minute rule dictates that speech and occupational therapists must provide at least 8 minutes of direct, one-on-one treatment to bill for a single 15-minute unit under Medicare Part B. Total timed minutes per day are aggregated and divided by 15; a remainder of **8 minutes or more** counts as an extra billable unit.


Other payers may use different methodologies, and code-specific instructions may apply. Routine preparation and documentation time generally do not count as direct treatment time. See ASHA's[guide](https://www.asha.org/practice/reimbursement/coding/understanding-timed-and-untimed-cpt-codes/) to timed and untimed CPT codes for additional guidance.


### CMS 8-Minute Unit Conversion Chart


Units Billed Total Treatment Minutes Required (Single or Combined Timed Codes)


0 Units 0 - 7 minutes


1 Unit 8 - 22 minutes


2 Units 23 - 37 minutes


3 Units 38 - 52 minutes


4 Units 53 - 67 minutes


5 Units 68 - 82 minutes


6 Units 83 - 97 minutes


7 Units 98 - 112 minutes


8 Units 113 - 127 minutes


### How Time Works for the New Speech Treatment Codes


Starting January 1, 2027, speech treatment is billed with timed codes for the first time. These codes follow a different structure from the chart above. Each base code covers the first 30 minutes. Under the general CPT midpoint convention,[ASHA](https://www.asha.org/practice/reimbursement/coding/new-speech-language-pathology-treatment-codes-replacing-92507/treatment-codes/) lists 16–37 minutes for one base code. For example, 48 minutes falls in the 38–52 minute range and supports a base code plus one add-on unit. A 55-minute session falls in the 53–67 minute range and supports a base code plus two.


These are CPT conventions, not Medicare's final word. NCCI and Medically Unlikely Edit requirements are expected in the last quarter of 2026.[ASHA](https://www.asha.org/practice/reimbursement/coding/understanding-timed-and-untimed-cpt-codes/) notes that CMS rules and payer policies may set different requirements, so check each payer's policy before billing.


## Defensible Documentation: Clinical Sentence Structures


Effective documentation must reflect the individual patient's presentation, the skilled service provided, the response to treatment, and progress toward measurable goals. Generic or copied language that does not accurately describe the encounter can jeopardize the record. The following sentence structures are ideas, not substitutes for individualized clinical documentation.


**Skilled need:**


Skilled need


The intervention required the skills of the {formmenu: SLP; OT} to provide {formtext: name=specific skilled intervention} because {formtext: name=documented impairment} limited the patient's ability to {formtext: name=specific functional activity}.


_


**Medical necessity:**


Medical necessity


Continued skilled therapy remains medically necessary because {formtext: name=documented impairment} limits the patient's ability to {formtext: name=functional activity}, requiring {formtext: name=specific skilled intervention} to address {formtext: name=identified safety or functional concern}.


_


**Progress toward goals:**


Progress toward goals


The patient progressed toward {formtext: name=measurable goal} by {formtext: name=specific observed performance} with {formtext: name=measured level of accuracy or assistance}, compared with {formtext: name=documented baseline}.


_


Whenever possible, describe the type and level of cueing or assistance provided, the patient's response, and objective changes from baseline. Include only details supported by the actual clinical encounter.
